note: The foundational indirect injection paper with a security taxonomy, still the clearest reference for explaining the risk to a client.
title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
journal: Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

reading.body:
Indirect prompt injection was demonstrated on real systems in 2023, and the paper that showed it remains the standard reference, with 1,988 citations.

The pattern is that an LLM application treats retrieved content as instructions rather than as data. An attacker who can place text in a webpage or document the application later fetches can steer that application without ever addressing it directly. The authors built a taxonomy of what follows: data theft, self-spreading attacks, polluted information, and control over app actions and API calls. They tested this on Bing Chat, on code completion engines, and on synthetic GPT-4 applications.

This matters for AI specifically because it inverts the usual trust boundary. A model that reads the web or a document store is doing exactly what it was built to do, and that reading is the attack surface. The paper's own conclusion is that effective mitigations remain scarce, which is why the note calls it the clearest way to explain the risk to a client.

What the data does not cover is the state of defenses after 2023. The citation count shows the paper is widely relied on, not that the problem was solved. Nothing here measures how often indirect injection occurs in production, what a fix costs, or whether any deployed system has closed the gap.

explain_beginner: This paper explains a new risk for apps that use large language models. Normally people think the user gives the instructions. The authors show that an attacker can instead place hidden instructions inside information the app later looks up, such as a webpage or document. Because the model may treat that data as commands, the attacker can affect the app without ever talking to it directly. The paper sorts these dangers into categories, including stealing data, spreading itself, and polluting information. It also tested real systems like Bing Chat and code helpers. The main point is that many current systems lack good defenses, so builders and users need to be careful.
explain_business: For executives, this paper warns that adding an LLM to a product creates a new security exposure. If the system reads outside content, such as web pages or documents, an attacker can hide instructions in that content and influence the application without direct access. The authors show this can lead to stealing data, attacks that spread themselves, polluted information, and control over app actions or API calls. They demonstrated the problem on real services, including Bing Chat, and on synthetic GPT-4 applications. Because effective defenses are still lacking, leaders should treat LLM integrations as risky and decide whether to deploy or rely on them before robust protections exist.
explain_practitioner: The authors study LLM integrated applications where retrieved content can be interpreted as instructions, not just data. They examine indirect prompt injection, where an adversary plants prompts in material likely to be fetched during inference, so no direct user interface is needed. They build a security taxonomy covering stealing data, self-spreading, polluted information, and other risks. They then test attacks on real systems, including Bing Chat and code completion engines, plus GPT-4 synthetic applications. The key result is that retrieved prompts can act like executable code, alter application behavior, and control whether and how other APIs are called. The paper notes effective mitigations remain scarce.
